items.note: This is the one section where mmHg belongs: it is the unit for the partial pressure of carbon dioxide and oxygen, not for electrolytes.

stage1.question: Which does this blood gas indicate?

options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis is a high pH with a LOW carbon dioxide: the patient is blowing off too much. pH and carbon dioxide move in opposite directions. That is not the pattern here.
Metabolic acidosis is a low pH with a LOW bicarbonate: acid gained or base lost. pH and bicarbonate move in the same direction. That is not the pattern here.
Metabolic alkalosis is a high pH with a HIGH bicarbonate: base gained or acid lost. pH and bicarbonate move in the same direction. That is not the pattern here.
The pH is low and the carbon dioxide is high, moving in opposite directions. Respiratory Opposite. The bicarbonate is still normal, so this is uncompensated.

stage2.question: Which findings do you expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drowsiness, confusion, and a declining level of consciousness
options.rationale: Retained carbon dioxide is a central nervous system depressant.
Carbon dioxide dilates cerebral vessels.
Hypoventilation is the cause, not the compensation.
Acidosis drives potassium out of cells, so the serum level climbs without the body gaining any.

options.text: Tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips
options.rationale: That belongs to respiratory alkalosis. Alkalosis binds more calcium to albumin, so the free calcium falls and nerves become irritable.

options.text: Carpal spasm without a low serum calcium
options.rationale: That belongs to respiratory alkalosis. The ionized calcium fell even though the total is normal. The treatment is the breathing.

stage2.scoring: All correct options and no incorrect options.

items.takeaway: ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal. Read the pH, then the carbon dioxide, then the bicarbonate, then decide the compensation.

stage2.question: Which statements about this result are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The normal range is 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL
options.rationale: The range worth memorizing for this test.

options.text: A value below 9 mg/dL would be hypocalcemia
options.rationale: Calcium blocks sodium channels on the nerve membrane. Take it away and nerves fire on their own.

options.text: A value above 10.5 mg/dL would be hypercalcemia
options.rationale: Extra calcium seals the membrane shut. Sodium cannot get through and cells will not depolarize.

options.text: A normal value here rules out every problem with this electrolyte
options.rationale: It does not. A value can be normal while the patient is compensating, while a related value is abnormal, or while the level is falling rapidly toward trouble.

options.text: This result still has to be read alongside the related values
options.rationale: Potassium is read with magnesium, calcium with phosphorus and albumin, and any of them with the pH.

options.text: A single normal result means no further monitoring is needed
options.rationale: Trend matters more than a single point, especially in a patient receiving fluids, diuretics, or replacement.
